text.p: The Russian government is sure it will cope with the huge debt payments which fall in the years around the turn of the century, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Monday.
"Our estimates take into consideration the big payments," First Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin told Reuters.
"Keeping the debt and the volume of servicing at a certain level will allow us to make the payments easily. We do not have specific worries about that."

Russia's debt payments to the London Club of commercial bank creditors and to the Paris Club of official creditors will peak in 2002, when it will have to pay about $12 billion. In 1997 Russia will have to pay $9.2 billion.
In 2002 Russia will also have to repay $1 billion when its first Eurobond issue matures.
Russia's payments on a $10 billion credit from the International Monetary Fund will peak in 1998 and 1999.
Kudrin said Russia would not have to increase foreign borrowing to repay the debts as the government was now able to make long-term borrowings on international markets.
Russia is now holding a road-show for its third Eurobond, which is likely to run for 10 years. Its first Eurobond had a five-year term and the second one seven years.
Previously a Finance Ministry official said Russia could issue 20 to 30-year paper this autumn.
Kudrin said foreign debt servicing would account for the lion's share of Russia's budget deficit in 1998.

President Boris Yeltsin said recently Russia's 1998 budget deficit would amount to 5.5 percent of gross domestic product and Kudrin said debt servicing would account for five percentage points of this.
In 1999 the deficit will be due entirely to debt servicing, with the government running a balanced budget as far as primary spending is concerned.
